youtube.title: Why Did Coca-Cola Change Its Formula in 1985?
youtube.description:
In 1985 Coca-Cola replaced the formula it had sold for 99 years. In nearly 200,000 taste tests more people picked the new one, and the country still turned on it. Why did New Coke win the tests and lose America?

This documentary follows the decision from the slide in market share and the Pepsi Challenge to Project Kansas, the Lincoln Center launch, the flood of calls and letters, and the 79 days that ended with Coca-Cola Classic back on the shelves, with the company's own words on screen.

{CHAPTERS}

sources.claim: Coca-Cola announced the new formula on 23 April 1985 at Lincoln Center in New York
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', coca-colacompany.com, 14 Nov 2012; New York Times, 24 Apr 1985

sources.claim: The change was on the front page of The New York Times on 24 April 1985
sources.source: The New York Times, front page, 24 Apr 1985

sources.claim: The original formula's return was announced on 11 July 1985, as Coca-Cola Classic (79 days after the launch)
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', 2012

sources.claim: Coca-Cola was first mixed by a pharmacist in Atlanta in 1886 (99 years before the change)
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, company history, coca-colacompany.com; Mark Pendergrast, For God, Country and Coca-Cola (1993)

sources.claim: Coke's share of the US soft drink market fell from about 60 percent just after the Second World War to less than 24 percent in 1983
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', 2012

sources.claim: In 1984 the company's revenue was more than seven billion dollars
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, Annual Report 1984

sources.claim: Roberto Goizueta, a chemical engineer born in Cuba, became chairman in 1981 and told managers nothing would be sacred
sources.source: Mark Pendergrast, For God, Country and Coca-Cola (1993); New York Times obituary of Roberto Goizueta, 19 Oct 1997

sources.claim: Coke's 1982 slogan was 'Coke is it!'
sources.source: Mark Pendergrast, For God, Country and Coca-Cola (1993)

sources.claim: Pepsi marketed itself to younger drinkers through the Pepsi Generation campaign from 1963
sources.source: Mark Pendergrast, For God, Country and Coca-Cola (1993)

sources.claim: The Pepsi Challenge, filmed blind taste tests, began in Dallas in 1975 and more participants picked Pepsi
sources.source: Mark Pendergrast, For God, Country and Coca-Cola (1993); Roger Enrico and Jesse Kornbluth, The Other Guy Blinked (1986)

sources.claim: Coke's own blind tests also often favoured Pepsi
sources.source: Thomas Oliver, The Real Coke, the Real Story (1986)

sources.claim: Coke led in restaurant fountains and vending, while Pepsi was gaining in supermarkets
sources.source: Mark Pendergrast, For God, Country and Coca-Cola (1993)

sources.claim: Pepsi signed Michael Jackson and his brothers for its ads in a deal reported at five million dollars, aired in 1984
sources.source: Roger Enrico and Jesse Kornbluth, The Other Guy Blinked (1986); Pendergrast (1993)

sources.claim: Diet Coke launched in 1982, the first extension of the Coca-Cola trademark, and by 1984 was the third best-selling soft drink in the US
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, company history (Diet Coke); Pendergrast (1993)

sources.claim: The reformulation was code-named Project Kansas and produced a smoother, sweeter formula
sources.source: Thomas Oliver, The Real Coke, the Real Story (1986); The Coca-Cola Company, 2012

sources.claim: The original recipe was kept in an Atlanta bank vault from 1925
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'Coca-Cola Moves Its Secret Formula to the World of Coca-Cola', 8 Dec 2011

sources.claim: Nearly 200,000 consumer taste tests
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', 2012

sources.claim: The new formula beat the old one in blind tests, roughly 55 to 45 by one account; accounts of the margins vary
sources.source: Thomas Oliver, The Real Coke, the Real Story (1986); figures differ in Pendergrast (1993)

sources.claim: The new formula also beat Pepsi in blind tests
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 2012; Oliver (1986)

sources.claim: Development cost about four million dollars
sources.source: Mark Pendergrast, For God, Country and Coca-Cola (1993)

sources.claim: Sip tests tend to favour the sweeter drink
sources.source: Malcolm Gladwell, Blink (2005), discussing the Pepsi Challenge and New Coke

sources.claim: About 10 to 12 percent of tasters said they would be angry and alienated if the old Coke were taken away, and the research suggested that anger could influence others
sources.source: Thomas Oliver, The Real Coke, the Real Story (1986); Pendergrast (1993)

sources.claim: Selling two Cokes side by side was rejected for fear of splitting shelf space and burdening bottlers
sources.source: Thomas Oliver, The Real Coke, the Real Story (1986)

sources.claim: The new drink took the Coke name and the original formula was retired
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', 2012

sources.claim: Chairman's words at the launch: 'Some may choose to call this the boldest single marketing move in the history of the packaged-goods business. We simply call it the surest move ever made.'
sources.source: Roberto Goizueta, press conference, 23 Apr 1985, quoted in Pendergrast (1993)

sources.claim: Executives struggled at the launch to explain why the formula changed
sources.source: Mark Pendergrast, For God, Country and Coca-Cola (1993); Oliver (1986)

sources.claim: Within 24 hours, 81 percent of the US population knew of the change
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', 2012

sources.claim: Pepsi's ad, signed by Roger Enrico, president of Pepsi-Cola USA: 'After 87 years of going at it eyeball to eyeball, the other guy just blinked.' Pepsi gave employees a day off
sources.source: Roger Enrico and Jesse Kornbluth, The Other Guy Blinked (1986); Pepsi newspaper advertisement, 23 Apr 1985

sources.claim: Early sales of the new formula were good
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', 2012

sources.claim: By June 1985 the consumer hotline took 1,500 calls a day, against about 400 a day before the change
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', 2012

sources.claim: More than 40,000 calls and letters
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', 2012

sources.claim: Letters addressed to 'Chief Dodo, The Coca-Cola Company'
sources.source: Mark Pendergrast, For God, Country and Coca-Cola (1993)

sources.claim: A psychiatrist hired by the company to listen to calls said some callers sounded as if they were discussing the death of a family member
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', 2012

sources.claim: A man in San Antonio bought about $1,000 worth of the old Coke
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', 2012; Pendergrast (1993)

sources.claim: A retired investor in Seattle founded Old Cola Drinkers of America
sources.source: Mark Pendergrast, For God, Country and Coca-Cola (1993)

sources.claim: Bottlers pressed the company to bring the original back; company polling soured through June
sources.source: Thomas Oliver, The Real Coke, the Real Story (1986)

sources.claim: ABC News interrupted General Hospital to report the return
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', 2012

sources.claim: Senator David Pryor of Arkansas spoke of the return on the Senate floor as a meaningful moment in American history
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', 2012; Congressional Record, July 1985

sources.claim: Keough: 'The simple fact is that all the time and money and skill poured into consumer research on the new Coca-Cola could not measure or reveal the deep and abiding emotional attachment to original Coca-Cola felt by so many people.'
sources.source: Donald Keough, Coca-Cola president, press conference, 11 Jul 1985, quoted in The Coca-Cola Company, 2012

sources.claim: Keough: 'Some cynics will say that we planned the whole thing. The truth is we are not that dumb, and we are not that smart.'
sources.source: Donald Keough, press conference, 11 Jul 1985, quoted in The Coca-Cola Company, 2012

sources.claim: By the end of 1985 Coca-Cola Classic was outselling both New Coke and Pepsi
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, 'The Real Story of New Coke', 2012

sources.claim: New Coke was renamed Coke II in 1990 and discontinued in the US in 2002
sources.source: Mark Pendergrast, For God, Country and Coca-Cola, 3rd ed. (2013)

sources.claim: Roger Enrico became PepsiCo's chief executive in 1996
sources.source: PepsiCo, Annual Report 1996

sources.claim: Goizueta led the company until his death in 1997; its market value grew from about $4 billion to about $145 billion under him
sources.source: New York Times obituary of Roberto Goizueta, 19 Oct 1997

sources.claim: New Coke returned briefly in 2019 with Netflix's Stranger Things, set in 1985
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company press release, 21 May 2019

sources.claim: More than 2.2 billion servings of the company's beverages a day
sources.source: The Coca-Cola Company, Form 10-K for fiscal 2023, filed Feb 2024

sources.claim: Netflix announced Qwikster in September 2011 and dropped it in October 2011
sources.source: Netflix blog posts, 18 Sep 2011 and 10 Oct 2011
